reference.source: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A behavioural syndrome resulting from bilateral damage to the medial temporal lobes, particularly the amygdalae
Core features include hyperorality (examining and placing objects in the mouth), hypersexuality, and abnormal placidity or blunted fear and anger
Visual and other agnosias may occur, with an inability to recognise objects or their significance (psychic blindness)
Hypermetamorphosis, an excessive tendency to attend and react to every visual stimulus, is characteristic
In humans the full syndrome is uncommon and often partial, arising from herpes simplex encephalitis, head injury, stroke, frontotemporal dementia, or after temporal lobectomy
Memory impairment frequently accompanies the syndrome because of medial temporal involvement
Management is supportive and directed at the underlying cause, with behavioural measures and cautious pharmacotherapy for disruptive symptoms
reference.pathophysiology: Kluver-Bucy syndrome follows bilateral destruction or dysfunction of the anterior temporal lobes and amygdalae, structures central to assigning emotional and biological significance to sensory stimuli. Loss of amygdala function disconnects perception from appropriate emotional appraisal, producing tameness and loss of fear (placidity), indiscriminate oral and sexual exploration, and an inability to attach meaning to what is seen despite intact primary vision. Involvement of adjacent hippocampal and temporal cortex accounts for the accompanying amnesia and agnosia. In humans the commonest cause is herpes simplex encephalitis, with other aetiologies including trauma, infarction, neurodegeneration, and bilateral temporal surgery.
additionalDifferentials: Herpes simplex and other limbic encephalitis
Post-ictal or interictal behavioural change in temporal lobe epilepsy
Hypersexuality from medication or endocrine disorder
additionalInvestigations: MRI brain to demonstrate bilateral temporal or amygdala lesions
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis and viral PCR for herpes simplex and autoimmune encephalitis
Electroencephalography to assess for temporal epileptiform activity
Autoimmune and paraneoplastic antibody panel where encephalitis is suspected
Neuropsychological assessment of memory, recognition, and behaviour
redFlags: Fever, headache, and altered consciousness suggesting active encephalitis requiring urgent treatment
Rapidly progressive behavioural change pointing to autoimmune or neurodegenerative disease
Hypersexual or disinhibited behaviour posing risk to the patient or others
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the underlying cause; features following herpes simplex encephalitis or extensive bilateral injury may be permanent, whereas some post-ictal or reversible cases improve. Residual memory and behavioural impairment commonly persists.
pitfalls: Failing to recognise and treat herpes simplex encephalitis promptly as an underlying cause
Mistaking the disinhibition for primary psychiatric illness
Overlooking accompanying amnesia and agnosia when assessing capacity and safety
Attributing hyperorality or hypersexuality to behavioural choice rather than organic disease
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Treat the underlying cause, with aciclovir for herpes simplex encephalitis and immunotherapy for autoimmune encephalitis
Structured behavioural management and supervision for hyperorality, hypersexuality and disinhibition
Pharmacological control of behavioural symptoms with antipsychotics, mood stabilisers such as carbamazepine, or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors for hypersexuality and aggression
Environmental safety measures, including removing hazardous objects given indiscriminate oral exploration
Neurorehabilitation with cognitive and memory support
Antiseizure medication where temporal lobe seizures occur
Multidisciplinary neurology and neuropsychiatry input with carer education and support
